The main differences concern the interpretation of the pronouns and the phrase 'from before and from behind', and the commentators do not settle between these readings.

The verse warns the disbelievers that if they turn away, they will be struck by a thunderbolt-like punishment like the one that befell ʿAd and Thamud. Commentators differ on the phrase 'from before them and from behind them': al-Tabari holds that it refers to the messengers sent before and after the prophets, while Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi take it to refer to ʿAd and Thamud themselves. Az-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan understand it as an intense, all-sided effort at persuasion, and al-Hasan as warnings about both past and future punishments. All agree that the messengers' call was the same: to worship God alone. Their reply, 'Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels,' is read by al-Tabari and al-Nasafi as a rejection of a human messenger, while al-Razi and Ibn ʿAshur see it as denying the prophethood of humans altogether. Az-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy consider their closing words, 'we disbelieve in what you were sent with,' to be mockery rather than acknowledgment, and Ibn ʿUthaymin adds that the emphatic wording shows obstinacy. Regarding ʿAd, the scholars describe a cold, violent and noisy wind, and Thamud was struck by a shout and an earthquake, as al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report. Accounts of the inauspicious days vary, and the Meccans knew the stories of these peoples from their journeys, as Ibn Juzayy notes.

This verse tells of the people of 'Ad, the people of Hud, who were arrogant on earth without right. When Hud threatened them with punishment, they trusted in their strength and great bodies and said: who is stronger than us? God answers that He who created them is stronger than they are, since it is He who gave them their strength, and that they denied signs whose truth they knew. The commentators report that they were very tall and that a man could tear a rock from a mountain with his bare hands. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi agree that strength belongs to God, and that a person is strong only by the power God grants him. On the meaning of the harsh wind, they differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and 'Ikrima took it to be a bitterly cold wind, Mujahid a scorching one, and al-Suddi and Abu 'Ubayda a loud one. Ibn Kathir holds that it combined all these qualities. On the days described as ill-omened, Mujahid and Qatada said they were unlucky days running in succession from the end of Shawwal, while others described them as violent or dust-laden. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur note that the punishment of the Hereafter is more degrading than that of this world, and that no one will come to their aid. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan point out that their ruin came through the wind, God choosing a means that people think trivial to show His power.

This verse describes how God sent a violent wind against the people of 'Ad, on days of misfortune, in order to make them taste the humiliation of this world, while the punishment of the Hereafter is still more humiliating and they will have no helper. On the nature of the wind, the commentators agree that it was violent and fierce. Mujahid says it was scorching, while Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi say it was cold, and al-Tabari and others stress that it made a loud, startling noise. Some combine these meanings into one wind that was harsh, cold and roaring. The word nahisat is read in two ways: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a sukun on the ha, the others with a kasra. Al-Tabari considers both readings well known and of the same meaning. As for its sense, Mujahid and Qatada take it as ill-omened days, Ibn 'Abbas as consecutive days, and al-Dahhak as severe days; some say they were dusty. Many report that the days ran from the last Wednesday of Shawwal to the next Wednesday, though al-Shinqiti rejects any general belief that Wednesdays are unlucky. Ibn al-Qayyim adds that a day can be unlucky for some and lucky for others.

This verse says that God made the way of truth clear to the people of Thamud and guided them to it, but they chose blindness over guidance, meaning they preferred misguidance and disbelief to faith. So the seizing thunderbolt of humiliating punishment struck them because of what they had earned: disbelief, denial of the messengers, and the slaughtering of the she-camel. The commentators agree that guidance here means guidance by clarification and indication, not guidance by granting success, as reported from Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as pointing out both paths, good and evil, and al-Alusi prefers this sense because it fits the phrase about choosing blindness. Al-Tabari explains the verb as choosing, while Ibn Atiyya and others read it as a choice that is nonetheless contained in God's decree. On the word sa'iqa, al-Suddi takes it to be fire, Marwan ibn al-Hakam a cry from heaven, and Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari a cry together with a violent quake; al-Alusi combines fire and cry. Al-Hawn means humiliation and describes the punishment or stands in apposition to it. The readings of the name Thamud differ in case and in the presence of tanwin, and al-Tabari prefers the nominative without tanwin. The verse closes with the deliverance of those who believed and were mindful of God.

This verse states that God delivered those who believed, meaning the believers among the people of Thamud who followed their prophet Salih, and who were mindful of God. The commentators explain that God had shown Thamud the path of truth and error, but they chose blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of humiliating punishment struck them for what they had earned through denial and the slaying of the she-camel. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that the believers are Salih and those who followed him, and that the deliverance concerned that thunderbolt. Al-Baghawi, Abu al-Su'ud, Ibn Ashur and al-Shinqiti treat the verse as the conclusion of the account of 'Ad and Thamud, contrasting the rescue of the believers with the destruction of the others. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi explain that piety here means avoiding polytheism and sins, while Ibn Ashur sees it as a constant habit of God-consciousness. Al-Razi and Ibn Uthaymin draw the point that faith alone is not enough without piety. The disagreements concern the meaning of the thunderbolt and the humiliating punishment, not the general sense of the verse.

This passage of Surat Fussilat describes the gathering of God's enemies toward the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. The commentators explain that the first of them is held back until the last catches up with him, an image of their great number and forced driving. The meaning of the verb 'yuza'un' is given by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as being held back, by Ibn Abbas as being pushed, by Ibn Zayd as being driven, and by Mujahid as being stopped. When they reach the Fire, their hearing, sight and skins testify against them about what they did. They then rebuke their skins, which reply that God, who makes everything speak, made them speak, the One who created them the first time and to whom they will return.

Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi, understand 'the skins' as the skins themselves, while as-Suddi, Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far and al-Farra' take them to mean the private parts, a view al-Tabari considers less likely. Ibn Abbas, as reported by al-Mawardi, means the hands and feet, and al-Zamakhshari adds that the limbs in general are meant. Al-Razi explains the choice of hearing, sight and touch by the fact that most sins are committed through these senses. On the verb 'yastatirun', Mujahid reads it as 'fearing', Qatada as 'supposing', as-Suddi as 'hiding', and several link the verse to the report of Ibn Mas'ud about three men near the Ka'ba who doubted that God hears their words. The commentators agree that the false opinion about God brought these people to ruin, that the inhabitants of the Fire will not leave it whether they endure or not, and that their request to be pleased will not be granted.

This passage describes the gathering of Allah's enemies toward the Fire: according to the commentators, they are driven forward and the first of them is held back until the last have caught up. When they reach the Fire, their hearing, their sight and their skins bear witness against them about what they did in the world. The commentators agree on the core meaning: the body parts speak by Allah's will, since the One who made everything speak is able to make them speak on the Day of Resurrection; the disbelievers hid their sins while assuming that Allah did not know much of what they did, and this assumption led to their ruin. As for the word "skins", most scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, take it literally as the skins themselves, while al-Sudi, Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far and al-Farra' read it as a euphemism for the private parts; al-Tabari judges this sense less familiar, and Ibn Juzayy regards the apparent meaning as the stronger one. On the meaning of "hiding", Mujahid explains it as guarding oneself, Qatada as supposing, and al-Sudi as concealment, while Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the word admits two readings. Most cite the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud about three men at the Ka'ba as the occasion of revelation, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya suggests the verse may date from after the conquest of Mecca. On the phrase "if they endure, the Fire is their dwelling", the commentators explain that patience will not help them and that their plea for reconciliation will not be granted. Al-Razi offers three ways of understanding the testimony: Allah creating understanding and speech within the limbs, creating sounds that convey meaning, or the limbs displaying signs of the deeds, and he acknowledges the difficulty without deciding among them.

The verse describes a scene of the Day of Judgment: God's enemies are gathered toward the Fire, their first ranks held back until the last have caught up. When they reach it, their hearing, sight and skins testify against them. They rebuke their skins, which reply that God, who makes everything speak, made them speak, and that He created them the first time and is the One to whom they will return. The commentators agree that the testimony is real and that the speech comes from God's power. Most understand 'skins' literally, while al-Suddi, Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far and al-Farra' take it as a euphemism for the private parts; Ibn al-Athir and others find this reading more eloquent. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and others explain the phrase 'you used to hide' as 'you concealed yourselves', Mujahid as 'you feared', and Qatada as 'you thought'. Several, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, hold that these people believed God did not know much of what they did, and that this belief was their ruin. The tradition transmitted through Ibn Mas'ud links the verse to three men who discussed, inside the Ka'ba, whether God could hear their words. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi stress the seriousness of this bad opinion of God. Al-Razi also weighs how the testimony happens without settling the question, noting that it is a difficult point for the Mu'tazila. On the request to make amends, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy conclude that the Fire will be their dwelling and that their plea will not be granted.

This passage describes the scene in which the enemies of God are gathered toward the Fire, with the first held back until the last catch up. When they arrive, their hearing, sight and skins testify against them. When they rebuke their skins, the skins answer that God, who makes everything speak, made them speak, and He created them the first time and to Him they will return. The phrase "you did not conceal yourselves" is explained by most commentators as meaning that they hid their sins; Mujahid reads it as guarding oneself, Qatada as supposing, and al-Suddi as concealing oneself from one's own body. The commentators agree that the root of their boldness in sin was the belief that God does not know much of what they do, and that this false opinion ruined them. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir treat it as disbelief or close to it. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse was linked to some Qurayshites who whispered in the Ka'ba, which Ibn Mas'ud overheard and reported to the Prophet, while al-Tabari reads it in general terms. The verb yasta'tibu means to seek to be pleased again or to return; most agree that their plea will not be granted, and that the Fire will be their dwelling whether they endure or not. On the meaning of "julud", most take it as the ordinary skins, Ibn 'Abbas and others as the private parts, and others as the hands and feet.

This verse teaches that the bad opinion the disbelievers held of God destroyed them: they believed He did not know much of what they did, so they dared to disobey and hid their deeds, and that belief became the cause of their ruin and loss. Al-Tabari explains that 'ardakum' means 'brought you to destruction', and he quotes al-Hasan al-Basri saying that people act according to their opinion of their Lord: the believer who thinks well of God acts well, while the disbeliever and hypocrite who think badly act badly. The commentators agree on the main point: thinking that God does not know hidden deeds leads to ruin, and on the Day of Judgment the hearing, sight and skins will testify against the one who disobeyed. Ibn Mas'ud is reported to have explained the occasion of revelation: three men speaking secretly near the Ka'ba doubted that God heard them, and the verse was revealed. On the word 'skins', most understand the skins themselves, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi take it as a reference to the private parts; Mujahid and Qatada explain that 'concealing' means guarding oneself or assuming. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan discuss the grammar, with 'dhalikum' as subject and 'ardakum' as predicate. Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Biqa'i draw the lesson that any opinion about God not sanctioned by revelation destroys its holder. For the end of the verse the commentators agree that the Fire is their dwelling and that asking for pardon will not help them, although some read the verb in the passive form.

This verse states the final fate of the disbelievers led to Hell: whether they endure patiently or complain, the Fire is their dwelling. Most commentators agree that patience will not benefit them and that their plea for redress will not be granted. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the word istiʿtab means asking to be returned to the world to make amends, and that this request is refused, citing the verse in which the damned cry, "Our Lord, bring us out of it." Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya take the word to mean asking for satisfaction or pardon, which God does not grant because they do not deserve it. Al-Zajjaj and al-Baghawi understand utba as contentment, and Tha'lab notes that ʿataba means to be angry and aʿtaba to be pleased. Al-Sam'ani says neither patience nor distress will help them. Some readers used the passive form, giving the sense that even if they were sent back they would return to what they had been forbidden, a view Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider possible. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that utba is the lifting of divine displeasure and that repentance is no longer accepted in the hereafter. Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn 'Ashur see the shift to the third person as a way of turning away from them. Ibn 'Uthaymin and Sayyid Qutb read in the verse the eternity of the punishment.

This part of the verse says that God assigned to the disbelievers companions from among the devils, both jinn and humans. These companions made attractive to them what lay before them, meaning the affairs of this world, its desires and visible sins, and what lay behind them, meaning the hereafter, leading them to deny resurrection and judgment. This verse reports that the disbelievers of Quraysh urged one another not to listen to the Qur'an when it was recited, and to make noise during its recitation so that it would be neither heard nor followed, hoping to overcome the Prophet. The commentators agree that Quraysh are meant and that the Prophet raised his voice when reciting in Mecca, drawing crowds, so the idolaters whistled, clapped and shouted to drown him out. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take this noise to be whistling, hand-clapping and confused talk, while Abu al-'Aliya understands the verb as slandering and disparaging the Qur'an, and al-Dahhak as multiplying words so that the reciter becomes confused. Al-Suddi adds that they shouted in his face. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir treat these explanations as closely related, all conveying obstruction and disturbance. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that lagh is speech with no benefit, and that the two readings of the verb are dialectal variants with one meaning. As for the punishment promised, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take it to refer to the Hereafter, and al-Qurtubi notes it is severe and unceasing, while others link it to the defeat at Badr. Al-Hasan holds that their good deeds are nullified by disbelief, so they are repaid only for their evil deeds. The commentators present these views side by side without weighing them against one another.

In this verse God swears that He will make those who disbelieve taste a severe punishment and will repay them with the worst of what they used to do. The context refers to the Meccan polytheists who agreed among themselves not to listen to the Quran and to drown out its recitation with noise. Commentators differ on when the punishment falls. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, takes the severe punishment to be the punishment of Badr in this world, while others, including Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, understand the worst repayment as the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the verb "to make taste" refers to a small measure that is experienced, so that even a small portion is severe, and the full amount is greater still. On the phrase "the worst of what they used to do", most explain it as repayment for their worst deeds, while al-Hasan holds that their good deeds are nullified by disbelief so that only their evil is counted. Al-Nasafi and al-Nisaburi identify that worst deed as polytheism. Ibn 'Ashur notes that "the abode of eternity" is the Fire itself, a figure of emphasis, and that denial of the signs is the cause of the idle noise. The commentators agree that the recompense of the Hereafter matches the deeds, and that disbelief is the gravest of sins, while differing on the timing and details of the punishment.

This verse states that the punishment just described is the due recompense of Allah's enemies: the Fire, where they will dwell forever as repayment for denying Allah's signs. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi, explain that "the Fire" clarifies the recompense and that "the abode of eternity" is the Fire itself, a figure of speech that stresses its everlastingness; al-Tabari supports this with a variant reading attributed to Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the phrase "in it" can also mean that the damned have a particular dwelling within the Fire. Scholars agree that the abiding is without end, and Ibn 'Uthaymin cites several verses to confirm this. The denial is taken as the reason for the punishment, and al-Zamakhshari explains that it is the cause of the noise and babble, mentioned just before, meant to drown out the Qur'an. According to most, the addressees are the polytheists of Mecca. The next passage, in which the disbelievers ask to see those who misled them, is read by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali and Qatada as referring to Iblis and Qabil, the son of Adam, who established disbelief and killing respectively, while al-Mawardi and al-Razi take it generically as any inciters of error among jinn and humans. Ibn 'Atiyya finds the first reading problematic, since the murderer was not an unbeliever.

This verse describes the words of the disbelievers in the Fire, who ask their Lord to show them the two who led them astray from among the jinn and mankind, so that they may trample them underfoot and see them at the lowest depth of the Fire. The commentators agree on the general meaning: these are the seducers, both jinn and humans, who made disbelief and sin look attractive. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi report, on the authority of Ali ibn Abi Talib and Qatada, that the two are Iblis and Qabil, the son of Adam, since the first established disbelief and the second established unjust killing. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi also transmit this view. Ibn Atiyya finds it hard to accept, because the son of Adam was a believer who disobeyed, whereas the speakers seek those who led them to eternal disbelief. Ibn Uthaymin prefers a general reading that does not restrict the verse to two individuals. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss the reading of 'arina': with a kasra it means 'show us', and with a sukun it means 'give us', according to al-Khalil. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that placing them under the feet means subjugation and humiliation, and reflects the anger these people feel toward those who misled them. Ibn Ashur notes that the mention of the lowest levels reflects their awareness that the seducers are deeper in the Fire than their followers.

This verse promises that those who declare that God is their Lord and then stand firm in their words and deeds will be visited by angels who bring them security and good news. Commentators differ on the meaning of steadfastness. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Mujahid take it as persisting in monotheism without associating anything with God. Umar, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada take it as persisting in obedience, performing the duties and avoiding sins, and Umar is reported to have said they did not swerve like foxes. Several, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir, combine the two, treating steadfastness as broader than the initial profession and covering both belief and action. On when the angels descend, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Abbas say at death, while Muqatil and Qatada say at resurrection. Many, and Ibn Kathir who calls this the most sound view, hold that it happens at death, in the grave and at resurrection together. Regarding the phrase do not fear and do not grieve, many explain that fear concerns what lies ahead in the hereafter and grief concerns what was left behind, and Ata' adds that it means reassurance that good deeds will be accepted and sins forgiven. The angels then say they are the believers' allies in this life and the next, and that they will have whatever their souls desire and ask for, as a welcome from a forgiving and merciful God.

The commentators explain that this verse records what the angels say to steadfast believers at death: "We are your allies in this world and in the Hereafter; there you will have whatever your souls desire and whatever you ask for, as a welcome from the Forgiving, the Merciful." They agree that istiqama (steadfastness) means holding firmly to monotheism, performing the obligations and avoiding what is forbidden. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report similar explanations attributed to Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, and al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari stress that this steadfastness goes beyond a verbal profession of faith. Scholars differ on when the angels descend: Mujahid and Ibn Zayd place it at death, Muqatil and Qatada at the resurrection, while Waki' and Ibn Kathir include all three stages: death, the grave and resurrection. On the meaning of "allies", al-Sudi and Mujahid identify them as the guardian angels who accompanied the believer in this life, whereas al-Razi understands a spiritual and inspiring influence that continues into the afterlife. "What you ask for" means what you wish for or request, and "nuzul" is the gift prepared for a guest, as al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi note.

The commentators explain that this verse describes what the angels promise to the believers who remain steadfast in the oneness of God and in obedience to Him: "We are your allies in this world and in the Hereafter, and you will have there whatever your souls desire and whatever you ask for." This is a nuzul, a prepared provision or hospitality for a guest, given by a Lord who is forgiving and merciful. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that nuzul means the provision or hospitality prepared for the visitor. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the angels guard the believers in this life and remain with them in the Hereafter until they enter Paradise; as-Suddi says they are the recording angels. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim explain this alliance as a spiritual influence of the angels on souls through inspiration and strengthening. The main disagreement concerns "what you ask for": Muqatil takes it as what you wish for, al-Razi as the spiritual Paradise, while az-Zamakhshari and al-Biqa'i distinguish what souls desire from what is requested. On istiqama, Abu Bakr and Mujahid understand steadfastness in monotheism, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada the performance of obligations and avoidance of sins, Umar a straightness without deviation, and Uthman sincerity in deeds. On when the angels descend, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd say at death, Muqatil and Qatada at resurrection, and Ibn Kathir joins these views into three moments: death, the grave and resurrection. Some commentators report that the verse was revealed about the muezzins, but most hold it general to every caller to God. Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi cite the hadith that no one enters Paradise by his deeds alone.

The commentators explain that this verse is a rhetorical question meaning a denial: there is no one whose words are better than those of someone who calls people to the worship of God, does righteous deeds, and declares that he is a Muslim. Most hold that the verse is general and applies to every caller to God who meets these conditions, as al-Hasan al-Basri, Muqatil, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur maintain, and that it includes prophets, scholars, fighters and preachers. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi record more specific views: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Sirin take it to refer to the Prophet ﷺ, while 'Aisha, 'Ikrima, Mujahid and Qays ibn Abi Hazim take it to refer to the muezzins, some of whom identify the righteous act with the two rak'ahs between the call to prayer and the iqama. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir consider these readings to fall within the general sense rather than exhausting it. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the phrase 'I am among the Muslims' expresses taking Islam as one's creed, and Ibn al-Arabi sees in it a verbal declaration of faith. For the following verses, the commentators give several meanings of good and evil: patience and anger, forbearance and abuse, pardon and retaliation, faith and polytheism. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report Ibn 'Abbas saying that one who responds this way is guarded from Satan and his enemy submits to him. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that some scholars regard this command as abrogated by the verse on fighting, while others hold it to remain in force. All agree that the whisper of Satan calls for seeking refuge in God.

This verse states that good and evil are not equal, and that one should repel evil with what is better. Whoever does so will see an enemy become almost like a close friend. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the address as directed to the Prophet ﷺ and to every caller to God, so that repaying wrongdoing with kindness and patience is what is asked. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the verse is general and includes anyone who calls to God, and al-Hasan takes it to mean any believer who answers God and calls others to obey Him. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi apply it to the Prophet ﷺ, while Qays ibn Abi Hazim, Aisha, Ikrima and Mujahid link it to the muezzins. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Arabi reply that the surah is Meccan while the call to prayer was instituted in Medina, so the verse cannot be limited to them. On the good and bad deed, opinions differ: faith and polytheism according to Ibn Abbas, forbearance and foul speech according to al-Dahhak, patience and aversion, or pardon and retaliation according to others. As for repelling with what is better, Ibn Abbas explains it as patience in anger, forbearance in ignorance and pardon for offence, while Mujahid and Ata' take it to mean giving greeting when meeting. Al-Qurtubi notes that some regard the verse as abrogated by the verse of fighting, while others do not. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the verse was revealed about Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who became a close friend after having been an enemy. Ibn Atiyya notes that the word 'as if' expresses comparison, since an enemy does not truly become an intimate friend. Al-Sa'di stresses kindness toward one who has wronged us, which demands great patience that only those of great fortune reach.

This verse teaches that answering evil with what is better is a noble quality, reached only by the patient, and granted only to one who has a great share of good. The commentators agree that good and evil are not equal, and that good deeds and bad deeds themselves differ in rank. Most explain that repelling evil with what is better means patience when angered, forbearance when faced with ignorance, and pardon when wronged, as reported by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy, and that this can turn an enemy into a warm friend. As for the "great share", Ibn 'Abbas understands it as abundant good and moral perfection, while Qatada and al-Hasan take it to mean Paradise, and others mean reward.

Opinions differ on what the good and the bad deed are. Ibn 'Abbas took them to be faith and polytheism, al-Dahhak forbearance and vulgarity, and others, such as al-Kalbi and Muqatil, gave different pairs, including gentleness and harshness, or pardon and retaliation. Regarding the preceding verse, al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd apply it to the Prophet ﷺ, 'A'isha, 'Ikrima, Mujahid and Qays ibn Abi Hazim to the muezzins, and al-Hasan himself to every believer who calls to God. Most favour the general sense, with muezzins included but not singled out.

As for the prompting of Satan, Ibn Zayd links it to anger, al-Suddi to inner whispering, and the verse commands seeking refuge in God, who hears and knows.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ that if a prompting from Satan reaches him, meaning a whisper or a goad that drives him toward anger, revenge, or neglecting what he was commanded, he should seek refuge in God, for He hears his plea and knows his state. Al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd explain the nazgh as a whisper and inner thought, Ibn Zayd also taking it to mean anger, and Ibn 'Abbas as the 'goadings'. Al-Zamakhshari links the verse to what precedes: if Satan turns you away from repelling evil with what is better, seek refuge in God and do not obey him. The preceding verses show that answering an offence with kindness is reached only by the patient, who possess a great share of good; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that this great share is Paradise, citing al-Hasan who said no share is greater than Paradise, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Tabari explain it as an abundant share of good. Al-Tabari relays the account of Abu Bakr insulted by a man, where the Prophet ﷺ told him that an angel had been defending him while he held back, and when he retaliated, the angel left and Satan came. Most commentators regard the verse as general to every believer, and Ibn Kathir notes that this passage has no parallel in the Quran except in Surat al-A'raf, with the emphasis varying by context. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that the emphatic pronoun here reflects how hard this command is for the soul.

The commentators explain that this verse counts the night, the day, the sun and the moon among God's signs, which demonstrate His power and oneness. Night and day follow each other in a fixed order, and the sun and moon move on a precise course. God then forbids prostration to them, because they are subjected creatures, and commands prostration to their Creator if one truly worships Him. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and others agree that the sun and moon are created beings that deserve no worship, and that their benefit comes from the subjection God imposes on them. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya report that some people prostrated before them while claiming to intend God by it, and it is this intermediary that is forbidden. As for the pronoun in 'khalaqahunna', most take it to refer to the four signs grouped as inanimate plurals, while others refer it to the sun and moon alone, or to the signs in general. Scholars differ on where the prostration falls: Malik, 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud place it after 'if you truly worship Him', whereas al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and Ibn 'Abbas place it after 'and they never tire'. The verse also mentions the angels who glorify God night and day without weariness. Most commentators see the revival of the dead land by rain as evidence for the resurrection.

This verse says that if the idolaters refuse to prostrate to God alone, the angels who are with your Lord do not turn arrogant towards worshipping Him. They glorify Him night and day without ever tiring, as al-Tabari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and the two Jalals explain. Ibn Abbas and Ibn 'Atiyya read this glorification as declaring God free from every flaw and devoting worship to Him alone. Al-Zamakhshari takes the phrase "with your Lord" to express dignity and closeness of rank rather than place, and al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur agree that it is a mark of honour. Al-Razi adds that this closeness belongs to certain distinguished angels. The commentators agree that glorification means worship and exalting God, while they differ on the meaning of "tiring": most take it as weariness and boredom, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi as boredom itself.

Scholars disagree about where the prostration in this verse falls. Malik places it at "worship Him", while Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i place it at "they do not tire". Al-Nasafi judges the second position the more cautious. Al-Suyuti and al-Alusi report that some Companions prostrated according to their own judgement.

The verse belongs to a passage on God's signs in creation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir present night, day, sun and moon as proofs of His power and wisdom, and stress that creatures must not be prostrated to. Ibn Kathir then turns to the sign of a dry earth stirred to life by rain, which most commentators read as evidence for resurrection.

This verse presents the earth as a sign of God's power: one sees it dry and barren, and when God sends down rain upon it, it stirs with plants and swells. The One who revives the earth can revive the dead, for He has power over all things. The commentators agree that 'khashi'a' describes the parched, plantless earth, and that 'stirring' refers to the movement of growing vegetation. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Suddi explain that the earth stirs with plants and swells with growth. Mujahid, followed by al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, holds that the swelling comes before the plants emerge, so the order of the words is reversed, while al-Kalbi and al-Sam'ani take the swelling to follow the appearance of the plants. Nearly all treat the sign as proof of resurrection: al-Tabari links the rain between the two blasts to the return of the dead, al-Razi reasons that scattered parts can be reassembled and given life again, and Ibn al-Qayyim speaks of reasoning by analogy. Ibn 'Ashur sees the whole passage as a comparison, and al-Qurtubi notes the reading 'rabat', attributed to Abu Ja'far, meaning 'rose up'. Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Jaza'iri stress the general nature of divine power, for which resurrection is no harder than the life of plants.

This verse addresses those who deviate from the truth concerning God's signs, distorting or denying them, and affirms that they are not hidden from Him and that His knowledge encompasses them. It then poses a rhetorical question: is one cast into the Fire better than one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection? The answer is obvious. The phrase "do what you will" is not a permission but a threat, since He sees everything you do.

The commentators agree that ilhad means deviating from the straight path, a usage drawn from digging a side-niche in a grave. They differ on the form this deviation takes. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, following Qatada, take it as denying the signs; Mujahid takes it as whistling, clapping and idle noise during the recitation; al-Sudi takes it as stubborn opposition; Ibn 'Abbas as placing speech out of its proper context; and Ibn Zayd as polytheism. Al-Tabari concludes that these meanings are closely related and that the verse encompasses them all, a view echoed by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya.

As for the two figures being contrasted, Ikrima and others name Abu Jahl and 'Ammar ibn Yasir, others name Abu Jahl and Hamza, 'Umar or 'Uthman, and Muqatil names the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Bahr read the verse as general. Several scholars, including Qatada, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, add that the Qur'an is protected from falsehood and alteration, and that no earlier or later scripture can refute it.

This verse states that those who disbelieved in the Reminder, meaning the Qur'an, when it came to them, will be lost or punished, and that the Book is mighty, meaning protected and made honourable by God. The commentators agree that the 'Reminder' is the Qur'an and that 'mighty' means invincible or noble in God's sight, as Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir report. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Suddi understand 'falsehood' to be Satan, who cannot take away any truth from the Qur'an or add any falsehood to it. Muqatil, al-Kalbi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr hold that earlier scriptures do not refute it and that no later book will cancel it. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Jurayj take it to mean that the Qur'an contains no error in its reports about the past or the future, while al-Razi draws from it that abrogation does not occur in it. As for the predicate of 'inna', most commentators supply an implied one, such as 'they will perish' or 'they will be punished'; others link it to 'they will be called from a distant place', and al-Zamakhshari treats the clause as an apposition to the preceding one. Ibn Kathir and others explain 'wise, praiseworthy' as wise in word and deed and worthy of praise. Most exegetes read the verse as a warning to the disbelievers and a consolation to the Prophet.

God declares that those who reject the Reminder, meaning the Quran, when it reaches them, will face the consequences of their disbelief, and that the Quran is a mighty and unassailable book. The commentators agree that the "Reminder" is the Quran, but they differ on the missing predicate of "inna": al-Kalbi, al-Tabari and others take it as an implied phrase meaning ruin or punishment, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' takes it to be "they will be called from a far place," al-Kisa'i holds that what precedes it stands in for it, and Ibn 'Atiyya prefers an implied predicate after "wise, praiseworthy." On the book's "might," Ibn 'Abbas understands it as its honour with God, Muqatil as its protection from Satan and falsehood, and al-Sudi as its uncreated nature. On "falsehood," Qatada, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Sudi identify it with Satan, Mujahid with distortion, and Ibn Jurayj with lies in its reports. Regarding "neither from before it nor from behind it," Qatada refers to earlier and later scriptures, Ibn Jurayj to its statements about past and future, while al-Tabari reads it as meaning that no deceiver can alter its meaning by his scheming. Al-Tabari concludes that the sense is that no one can change its meanings or add to it what is not part of it. "A revelation from the Wise, the Praiseworthy" is understood by most as a God who governs His servants wisely and is praised for His favours.

In this verse God consoles His Prophet ﷺ: what the disbelievers say to him, in rejection and insult, is not new, since the same words were said to the messengers before him. He must therefore be patient as they were patient. God is also abundantly forgiving toward those who repent, and holds a painful punishment for those who persist in disbelief until death. Most commentators read the verse as consolation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that earlier peoples called their prophets sorcerers or madmen, so the Prophet should endure as they endured. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir keep to the sense of rejection and harm. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi give a second sense: what is said to the Prophet is the same revelation that was given to earlier messengers, especially the message of forgiveness and punishment. Al-Razi considers the first sense the closer one and holds that the Prophet should leave the matter to God and continue his mission. He also links the verse to the preceding context of the disbelievers' words cited at the start of the surah. No commentator settles between these readings, and all agree on the core: the verse joins promise of forgiveness with warning of punishment, so that the believer keeps a balance between hope and fear.

This verse says that had the Quran been revealed in a foreign language, the disbelievers would have objected: why are its verses not made clear to us, a foreign book for an Arab messenger? The Prophet is told to reply that the Quran is guidance and healing for those who believe, while for those who do not believe there is deafness in their ears and blindness upon them, so they are like one called from a far place. The commentators agree that the Quran is Arabic, revealed in the language of its people, and that guidance and healing mean rescue from error and a remedy for doubt and ignorance. They differ on the calling from a far place. Mujahid and Ali understand it as distance from the hearts, which cannot grasp what they are called to. Al-Dahhak understands it literally, that on the Day of Resurrection they will be called by their worst names so that the whole assembly hears. Al-Farra compares it to someone who does not understand speech. As for the reading of the words a-a'jamiyyun, most readers take it as an interrogation of denial, while al-Hasan al-Basri and others read it without the question, so that the meaning becomes that some verses are foreign and others Arabic. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer the interrogative reading. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Razi note that the objections are presented as a hypothetical, showing that these people always find a pretext to reject the message, whatever form it takes.

The verse recalls that God gave Moses the Book, the Torah, and that his people then disagreed about it. Al-Tabari, al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi explain the disagreement as some believing in it and others rejecting it, and al-Tabari adds that it concerned putting its teachings into practice. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur note that Moses himself was denied and harmed. The phrase 'had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord' is understood by most commentators as the postponement of punishment until the Day of Resurrection, as al-Tabari, al-Suddi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi state. Al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi take it to mean that the people would have been annihilated, al-Biqa'i sees it as God's eternal decree, and Ibn Juzayy as divine destiny. Al-Qurtubi also reports that the delay may be due to believers who would emerge from their loins. The commentators agree that the disbelievers are meant by 'they are in a troubling doubt'. The word murib means a doubt that unsettles, and al-Tabari explains that they spoke without certainty, merely by conjecture. Ibn 'Ashur sees the passage as consolation for the Prophet, since what he faces is an old pattern with messengers. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri also suggest the pronoun may refer to the Torah or to Moses, but most refer it to the Qur'an.

The commentators explain that whoever does righteous deeds by obeying God and refraining from what He forbade gains the benefit for himself, namely Paradise and deliverance from the Fire, while whoever does evil by disobeying Him bears its consequence himself. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir add that God does not punish anyone except for a sin, and not before the proof has been established and a messenger sent. Ibn 'Atiyya sees in the verse a clear counsel, a warning and a promise, and holds that God never places any of His punishments outside their proper place. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi stress that God has no need of human obedience: the reward and the punishment both fall on the one who acts. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin hold that righteous deeds are those combining sincerity and conformity to revealed law, that evil deeds may include polytheism and blameworthy innovation, and Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that whoever initiates a bad practice bears its burden. Al-Shinqiti explains that the intensive form 'dhallam' may negate mere injustice, supporting this with other verses, while others read it as meaning 'one who is unjust'. Al-Sha'rawi sees in the verse the statement that God is a just judge between people and their own deeds. The commentators agree that the verse denies any injustice on God's part, that recompense follows from one's own earning, and that it belongs to the consolation of the Prophet facing his people's rejection.

This verse states that knowledge of the Hour belongs to God alone: when people ask about it, the answer is that only God knows it. The commentators add that God also knows what fruits emerge from their sheaths, what every female carries, and what she bears. The verse then describes the Day when God calls out to the idolaters, "Where are My partners?" They reply that they have informed Him that none of them bears witness to any partner, and that their deities have strayed from them and failed them.

The commentators agree on the general sense: the Hour is a matter that only God knows. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that the "akmam" are the coverings or sheaths that protect the fruit before it opens, and Ibn 'Abbas says this refers to the grape cluster before it blossoms. Al-Zamakhshari adds that God's knowledge includes the number of days and hours of pregnancy, whether the birth is premature or full-term, and the sex of the child.

The readings differ between "thamara" in the singular, read by the Kufans and others, and "thamarat" in the plural, read by the Medinans and Ibn 'Amir. Al-Tabari judges both valid since their meanings are close.

On the phrase "we have informed You," al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as a statement, al-Razi finds it hard to accept for a God who knows all, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan see it as a rhetorical reproach. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir take the word "dhann" here to mean certainty. Ibn al-Jawzi reports that the revelation was linked to a question the Jews put to the Prophet about the Hour.

The commentators explain that the verse describes the state of the polytheists on the Day of Judgment: the things they used to worship besides God vanish from them, are of no benefit, and cannot ward off anything, and they become certain that there is no escape from punishment. On the meaning of the verb “ẓanna” (ظنوا), most, including al-Sudde and Ibn Kathir, take it to mean “certainty”, while some grammarians, as al-Tabari reports, note that “mā” here is a negating particle so the verb has no effect on the object; others, such as al-Mawardi, hold that a remnant of hope may still remain for them. On “ādhannāka” (آذناك), Ibn Abbas reads it as “we informed you” or “we made you hear”, and al-Kalbi as “we informed you”, but Ibn Kathir and al-Razi find the notion of informing God unlikely, since the people of the Resurrection know that God knows all things. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi note that the speech may come from the polytheists or from their deities, and that its meaning is the denial of any testimony that God has a partner. Most link the passage to the theme that knowledge of the Hour belongs to God alone, and to His comprehensive knowledge that embraces fruits emerging from their sheaths and every pregnancy. The commentators see in the verse both a warning and a rebuke directed at the polytheists.

This verse describes the nature of the disbelieving human being, who never tires of asking for worldly good such as wealth and health, yet who, when touched by adversity, despairs and loses hope in God's mercy. The commentators agree that 'the human being' here means the disbeliever. Some report that the verse was revealed about al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, others about Utba ibn Rabi'a. Ibn Abbas draws the lesson that the disbeliever recognises his Lord in trial but not in ease. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi keep to this general sense. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan add that despair belongs to the heart, while the abjection (qunut) is what shows on the body. Al-Mawardi offers two readings: despair of good, or despair of having prayers answered, together with an evil opinion of one's Lord. Al-Razi observes that a person swings between pride in prosperity and collapse in hardship. All agree that the believer does not despair of God's mercy, a point supported by the verse: 'None despair of God's comfort except the disbelieving people.' No commentator decides between these readings; they simply set them out.

This verse describes the disbelieving person who, after being relieved of hardship by a blessing from God, such as health or wealth, claims that the good is due to him by his own merit and does not see it as a gift from God. Mujahid and Muqatil explain his words "this is mine" as meaning that it comes through his deeds and that he deserves it, while al-Zajjaj takes it to mean that it is a benefit he earned. His statement "I do not think the Hour will come" is read by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi as a denial of resurrection, whereas al-Tabari also notes that it may be a supposition. He then imagines that if he is brought back to his Lord he will have the best reward with Him. Several commentators, including al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Ali as cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, report that the disbeliever has two wishes, one in this world and one in the next, where he will wish he had been dust.

There is broad agreement that this presumption and self-exaltation are condemned, and that God announces He will inform the disbelievers of their deeds and make them taste a severe punishment. Al-Baghawi explains that this informing means showing them the evil of their deeds, and al-Zamakhshari reads it as a rebuke that confronts them with the reality of what they did. Ibn Ashur observes that the word "make them taste" is a metaphor that first raises hope and then discourages.

The differences concern mainly the wording. For "al-husna", some take it to mean Paradise, while others take it to mean a state of honour. On the occasion of revelation, al-Wahidi and al-Razi relate that it concerns al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, while al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi also mention other Meccan leaders such as Utba and Shayba ibn Rabi'a. Al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti note that the lam introduces an oath. Thus the interpretations of the terms vary, but the commentators all stress the arrogance and denial that the verse condemns.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the attitude of a person who, when God grants him blessings such as health or wealth, turns away from gratitude and withdraws with pride, but when harm touches him, he prays at great length. Al-Tabari and al-Sudde, followed by Ibn Kathir, explain that "ʿarid" means abundant, since the Arabs use length and breadth to mean quantity, as when one says someone prolonged his supplication. Ibn 'Abbas adds that the disbeliever recognises his Lord in hardship but does not know Him in ease, a view also reported by al-Sam'ani and al-Alusi. Al-Mawardi notes that turning away may mean turning from faith, from gratitude, or from obedience. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take "janb" as a figure for the self, meaning he departs in arrogance, while others keep the literal sense of bending the side. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as describing a general weakness of the human soul, except for those whom God protects, and he faults a person who calls on God only in distress when he should be thankful in ease. The readings "naʾa" and "naʾa" are said by all to have the same meaning. The scholars therefore agree that a person's conduct changes with his circumstances, while the exact nature of the turning away is debated among them.

God instructs His Prophet to put this question to those who reject the Qur'an: tell me, if this Book is from God and you disbelieve in it, who could be more astray than you, who are in a far-reaching opposition to the truth? Most commentators understand the question as a negation, meaning that no one is more misguided than they are, and as a rebuke. The word shiqaq denotes opposition and hostility. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the disbelief to mean rejecting the Qur'an, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the particle thumma implies a delay, so the disbelief came after reflection. Ibn 'Ashur adds that the address is first aimed at the common polytheists, since their leaders knew well that the Qur'an came from God. As for the next verse, which promises that God will show them His signs on the horizons and within themselves, the commentators differ on the meaning. Al-Sudd, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Tabari take it to mean the Muslim conquests around Mecca and the conquest of Mecca itself, while Qatada links it to the battle of Badr and to the punishments that struck earlier nations. Others, such as 'Ata', interpret it as the wonders of the heavens and the earth and the subtle design of the human body. Al-Tabari prefers the first view, because threatening the disbelievers with what they already see would make no sense. Finally, the statement that God is a witness over all things is taken by most exegetes to mean that His knowledge encompasses everything and that He will repay each person for their deeds.

This verse says that God will show the disbelievers His signs in the horizons and within themselves, until it becomes clear to them that the Quran is the truth, and then asks whether it is not enough that your Lord is a witness over all things. The commentators agree on the general sense: these signs are proofs that establish the truth of the revelation and of the Prophet's mission, and the future form introduced by the letter sin indicates that they will come soon. On the meaning of the horizons and the selves, however, opinions differ. Al-Sudi, Mujahid and al-Tabari understand the horizons to be the conquests of lands that God grants to the Prophet and the Muslims, and the selves to be the conquest of Mecca; al-Tabari favours this view, while Qatada links the selves to the battle of Badr. Ibn Zayd, Ata', al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi take the horizons to be the signs of heaven and earth, such as the sun, moon, stars and rain, and the selves to be the subtle workings of the human body, including how food and drink pass through it. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention the fate of earlier nations or bodily afflictions. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur suggest the words can carry several of these meanings at once. Grammatically, the clause that He is a witness over all things is treated as an appositive to 'your Lord'. Some read it as God's witness over the deeds of the disbelievers, others as His witness to the truth of the Quran, and others as His effective support for the Prophet.

This verse states that those who reject the Quran are in doubt about meeting their Lord, that is, about resurrection after death and return to God for judgment, and that God encompasses everything in knowledge and power. The commentators agree that the doubt here concerns resurrection and recompense. Al-Tabari and al-Sudi explain that these people doubt the coming of the Hour, so they neither work for it nor fear it. Ibn Kathir notes that whoever does not act for the Last Day behaves as though he doubts it. On the meaning of encompassing, al-Sudi takes it as encompassing knowledge of all things, while al-Kalbi takes it as encompassing power. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya combine both: God knows everything and has power over everything, and so He will repay the disbelievers for their disbelief and their doubt. Some readers pronounced the word mirya with a damma on the mim, a variant form that al-Zamakhshari treats as equivalent. Al-Razi links this closing statement to the whole surah, which opens with warning and closes with affirmation of resurrection and threat. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a comprehensive conclusion to the surah. The scholars agree on the general sense; they differ mainly over how far the idea of encompassing refers to knowledge and how far to power.
